children.value: This repository contains the guided notebooks for the Antarctica Datacube Hackathon. They introduce the ESA Antarctica Datacube and show how to discover Antarctic datasets, convert them into cloud-native formats, combine them into analysis-ready collections, and use those collections in scientific workflows.
Brief introduction to the hackathon, goals, EarthCODE context and agenda.
Dataset catalogue and one access notebook per source product.
Remote combined-cube access and examples for building a small cube.
Format conversion examples for Zarr, COG, GeoParquet, and the creation of STAC metadata.
Early visualisation experiments for interactive and static views.
Your hackathon solution space. Put new work here unless a challenge asks otherwise.
Create your own notebook or package here.

, which is ignored by Git. The canonical copies of the prepared assets live in cloud object storage.
- the data is available on EarthCODE’s
. The prepared assets demonstrate the path from domain-specific source products to cloud-native collections that can be inspected, combined, and cited.
The workflow to add data to these collections is to:
Start from a scientific product with its own native layout and metadata.
Convert or expose it as a cloud-native file format: Zarr for arrays, COG for rasters, GeoParquet for vectors and tables.
Add enough metadata for discovery, provenance, licensing, spatial extent, temporal extent, and variable interpretation.
Combine multiple products on a common analysis grid when that is scientifically defensible.

Why it matters in object storage
Multidimensional arrays such as time/depth/y/x cubes
Supports a flexible chunking scheme allows the indexing of data, optimised for analytics. Also, chunked reads let analysis load only the pieces it needs.
Single rasters or raster stacks exposed as files
Internal tiling and overviews enable efficient range reads and quicklooks.
Vector geometries and tabular point data
Columnar storage, embedded geospatial metadata, and fast filtering.

All the metadata generated for the datasets and hosted on the Open Science Catalog is in STAC format. The SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) specification was designed to establish a standard, unified language to talk about geospatial data, allowing it to be more easily searchable and queryable.
